newsitem.title: THAILAND: Markets to remain cool to Thai bank shares.
newsitem.headline: Markets to remain cool to Thai bank shares.

text.p: Respectable profits and more conservative lending practices are unlikely to reverse negative sentiment towards badly mauled bank and finance stocks on the fragile Thai stock market, analysts said on Monday.
Heavy selling of Thai blue-chip bank and finance counters by foreign institutional investors since early October has pushed the stock market to its lowest level in more than three years.
Since the start of October, the banking sector has declined 18.9 percent and finance and securities 27.5 percent. Share prices are still falling.

Analysts said even reports of encouraging third-quarter earnings expected for financial institutions would not allay market concern over Thailand's poor economic fundamentals and political uncertainty ahead of an election on November 17.

Bank profits, which account for almost half of all profits made by Thai listed companies, are widely expected to increase by eight to 10 percent over the year, below the 15 to 18 percent improvement forecast at the start of the year.
"I just don't think any numbers (results) will make a change in this market. No one really cares about results at the moment," said a senior bank analyst.
"The thing right now is the amount of money the institutions have in this market...Most other markets in Asia and Latin America are perceived as a better buy on political stability."

Thailand's economic growth is expected by many analysts to slow to around 6.8 percent this year from 8.6 percent last year, in part due to a slump in export growth to 5.5 percent in the first eight months of this year from 26 percent in 1995, they added.
With 70 percent of domestic borrowing coming through the Thai commercial banks, analysts said bank prospects were intrinsically linked to overall economic improvement.

"Thai banks are much stronger now, in terms of balance sheets, than at any time in the last two years," said Thanawat Patchimkul, banking analyst at Seamico Securities Plc. "But with the economic downturn, the problems must be seen as greater than in the past.
"While everything is looking cheap at the moment, we are expecting some more bad news over the next few months and don't see much of an improvement until this time next year."

Bank funding costs have risen after Moody's Investor Service downgraded the country's short-term sovereign debt rating from Prime-1 to Prime-2. Recent central bank curbs on overseas borrowing also have added to the cost of funds.
Some analysts said foreign banks were becoming cautious in lending to Thai banks.

Researchers said annual loan growth, capped by the central bank at 21 percent, was not likely to exceed 10 to 11 percent this year as the leading banks adopt more conservative lending practices in a weaker economic environment.
